newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Rao given week's reprieve in court case.
newsitem.headline: India's Rao given week's reprieve in court case.

text.p: Former Indian prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao won temporary reprieve in a criminal conspiracy case after police warned that militants could attack the political leader in Delhi's crowded courts.

Rao had been summoned to appear before a lower court judge on Monday to face charges and possible arrest in the $100,000 conspiracy case. He would have been the first former prime minister to appear in court in a criminal case.

The Supreme Court intervened after police said the teeming Tis Hazari court complex was vulnerable to extremist attacks despite the posting of hundreds of officers, some with sniffer dogs, around the sprawling site.

The high court ruled that Rao did not have to appear in court until it meets on October 7 to decide on the police demand that the venue of the lower court hearing be shifted to a more secure location.

Police had suggested the hearing be moved to a nearby sports stadium, a cavernous exhibition hall or a modern convention centre, all of which authorities said would be easier to defend and would accommodate the hundreds of interested journalists.
The lower court hearing was postponed to October 9.
The decisions gave Rao, who stepped down in disgrace on September 21 as leader of India's oldest party, Congress, a short period of grace before being formally charged.

Last week he was denied legal protection against arrest. If he is arrested, he can immediately seek bail. If arrested and denied bail, he will be put under either judicial or police custody pending trial.

The courts did not take up the substance of the allegations against Rao, who says he is innocent of accusations that he and a Hindu guru conspired in 1983 to cheat an expatriate Indian businessman of $100,000.

Last Thursday, federal police filed charges against Rao in a separate forgery case involving an alleged attempt in 1989 to tarnish the reputation of V.P. Singh, an opposition leader who later became prime minister.
Rao's abrupt resignation from the leadership of Congress, which has ruled India for all but four years since independence, has shaken Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's government.
Stock markets have fallen, anticipating tensions between Deve Gowda's centre-left minority coalition and Congress, which offers the prime minister make-or-break support in parliament.
New Delhi police chief Nikil Kumar told the court that intelligence reports indicated "serious threats to the security of Mr Rao existed", the Press Trust of India (PTI) reported.
The news agency said authorities were concerned over the presence of Sikh and Kashmiri militants in the capital waiting for a chance to mount a "sensational attack".

PTI quoted a police report as saying Tamil rebels and Islamic fundamentalists had in the past planned to target Rao, and that they could try to enter the court as journalists, lawyers or Rao supporters.
Former prime minister Indira Gandhi was shot dead by Sikh bodyguards in 1984. Her son, former prime minister Rajiv Gandhi, was blown up by a Tamil Tiger suicide bomber in 1991.
Police said there was no means of controlling access to the Tis Hazari labyrinth, which PTI said has five entrances, 250 courts and 70,000 visitors each day.
